coredata.dc:description: There is a balance between ionic conductivity and dimensional stability in anion exchange membranes (AEMs). High conductivity resulting from densely charged groups is normally accompanied with high water uptake and excessive swelling. Herein, a series of novel AEMs with interpenetrating network was prepared by the incorporation of poly(vinylbenzyl chloride) (PVBC) and poly(1-vinylimidazole)(PVIm) into the PVA matrix. PVBC and PVIm act as bifunctional macromolecular crosslinking agents to provide both imidazolium cations and to form crosslinked network in the membranes. The resulting AEMs were characterized by Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR), X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM). The effect of crosslinking density on conductivity, water uptake, swelling ratio and stability was investigated. The results reveal that the addition of PVBC-c-PVIm could be simultaneously conducive to higher conductivity and lower swelling ratio. Notably, the membrane containing 50wt% PVBC-c-PVIm had IEC of 1.86meqg−1, water uptake of 39.4%, and hydroxide conductivity of 21.9mScm−1 at 30°C. A maximum power density of 37.1mWcm−2 is achieved at a current density of 64mAcm−2. The crosslinked AEMs also exhibit excellent alkaline stability in a 4M KOH solution at 60°C for 1320h.

head.ce:title: Interpenetrating anion exchange membranes using poly(1-vinylimidazole) as bifunctional crosslinker for fuel cells

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: There is a balance between ionic conductivity and dimensional stability in anion exchange membranes (AEMs). High conductivity resulting from densely charged groups is normally accompanied with high water uptake and excessive swelling. Herein, a series of novel AEMs with interpenetrating network was prepared by the incorporation of poly(vinylbenzyl chloride) (PVBC) and poly(1-vinylimidazole)(PVIm) into the PVA matrix. PVBC and PVIm act as bifunctional macromolecular crosslinking agents to provide both imidazolium cations and to form crosslinked network in the membranes. The resulting AEMs were characterized by Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR), X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM). The effect of crosslinking density on conductivity, water uptake, swelling ratio and stability was investigated. The results reveal that the addition of PVBC-c-PVIm could be simultaneously conducive to higher conductivity and lower swelling ratio. Notably, the membrane containing 50wt% PVBC-c-PVIm had IEC of 1.86meqg−1, water uptake of 39.4%, and hydroxide conductivity of 21.9mScm−1 at 30°C. A maximum power density of 37.1mWcm−2 is achieved at a current density of 64mAcm−2. The crosslinked AEMs also exhibit excellent alkaline stability in a 4M KOH solution at 60°C for 1320h.

ce:section.ce:para: The emergence of fuel cells has significantly broadened the application of membrane technology due to its high energy efficiency and environmental friendliness [1,2]. Proton exchange membranes (PEMs), a key component for proton exchange membrane fuel cells (PEMFCs), have been attracting increasing attention in the last few decades because they possess high proton conductivity and excellent stability. Nevertheless, the commercialization is still impeded by some intrinsic weakness in PEMFCs, including limited oxygen reduction kinetics, poor selectivity and dependence on expensive catalysts (such as platinum) [3–5]. Hence, as an alternative, anion exchange membrane fuel cells (AEMFCs) are attracting increasing interest due to their incomparable advantages, such as the potential use of non-noble metal catalysts (silver and nickel) and their higher oxygen reduction kinetics than the PEMFCs [6,7].

AEMs with functional groups capable of transporting the hydroxyl anions are a key component in AEMFCs [2]. Recently, much effort has been devoted to the fabrication of three main types of AEMs including homogeneous, hybrid and interpenetrating network (IPN) membranes. Homogeneous AEMs, which are made from polymer material with cationic groups covalently bound to the polymer backbones, have been widely explored [8]. A variety of polymers with main chain structures such as poly(arylene ether)s [9], poly(olefin)s [10], polystyrene [11], poly(phenylene oxide) [12] and poly(phenylene) [13] have been reported. Hybrid membranes combine the features of both organic and inorganic materials, for instance PVA-SiO2 hybrid composites [14] and poly(arylene ether sulfone)-ZrO2 composites [15]. The third kind of AEMs belonging to (semi)IPN membranes generally have hydrophobic crosslinked network and hydrophilic linear main chain bearing functional cationic groups [16,17]. This characteristic often brings in good dimensional and chemical stability hence attracting growing research. A series of PVA-based (semi)IPN membranes has been reported recently such as PVA/QHECE [18], PVA/PDDA [19], and PVA/FP [20]. Although these AEMs display good stability and fabrication simplicity, their conductivity needs further improvement at relatively low water uptake.

Actually, there still exists universal antinomy in designing AEMs with excellent performance. In order to boost the ionic conductivity of the AEMs for practical application, enhancing the density of conductive groups such as quaternary ammonium [21], imidazolium [22], guanidinium [23], and phosphonium [24] is a straightforward method. Unfortunately, high ionic exchange capacity (IEC) usually results in excess water uptake, poor dimensional and mechanical stability as well. To conquer this trade-off, a versatile crosslinking approach can be employed. However, most of the crosslinking was realized at the expense of functional groups in AEMs, which inevitably causes a reduction in conductivity. Therefore, further exploration for an appropriate crosslinking agent is highly desirable.

Herein, we report the preparation a new kind of interpenetrating network AEMs, combining the attractive virtues of blend membranes and crosslinking technique. Initially, poly(vinylbenzyl chloride) (PVBC) was used as the hydroxide conducting polymer after being crosslinked with poly(1-vinylimidazole) (PVIm). Considering that the pristine crosslinked PVBC-c-PVIm is too brittle to be applicable in fuel cells, the cost-effective poly (vinyl alcohol) (PVA) was adopted as the matrix for its flexibility and good film forming property with excellent miscibility between other components [18,19,25]. PVA was treated with an amount of glutaraldehyde to promote its stability in an aqueous solution [19,26]. The novelty of this scheme stems from the fact that the macromolecular PVBC and PVIm acting as bifunctional crosslinkers in blend AEMs, can effectively suppress swelling by the formation of crosslinked network, and can simultaneously provide hydroxide conducting imidazolium groups, thereby facilitating desirable ionic conductivity. Moreover, the applied composite technique would have inspiring phenomena resulting from each blend component. Imidazolium is generally regarded to possess promising alkali resistance, the AEMs based on a polymerizable imidazolium salt reported by Li et al. [27] exhibit fairly good alkaline stability under high pH conditions although the conductivity is moderate. The new composite AEMs with various PVBC-c-PVIm contents were fabricated. The effect of crosslinking on IEC, conductivity, water uptake, swelling ratio, mechanical property and thermal stability was thoroughly discussed. We anticipate that this newly developed crosslinking strategy based on PVA matrix would tremendously contribute to the current trade-off dilemma.

Poly (vinyl alcohol) with a polymerization degree of
1750 ± 50
and hydrolysis degree of 98–99% was purchased from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co. Ltd. Poly (vinyl benzyl chloride) (60/40 mixture of 3- and 4- isomers with average molecular weight of Mn 55,000) was purchased from Sigma Aldrich. 1-Vinylimidazole (99%), 2,2-azobisisobutyronitrile (AIBN, 98%) and glutaraldehyde (GA, 50wt% aqueous solution) were commercially obtained from Aladdin Industrial Inc. The radical initiator AIBN was purified by recrystallizing from a methanol solution prior to use. CaH2 was stirred in N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF) (AR, Sinopharm, China) for 24h, distilled under reduced pressure and filtered over 4Å molecular sieves. All other chemicals were supplied from Shanghai Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd (China) and used as received.

Poly(1-vinylimidazole) (PVIm) was synthesized by the method described in the literature [28]. A typical process is summarized below. 4.0g of 1-vinylimidazole (42.5mmol) and 15mL of DMF were added into a 50mL three-necked round-bottomed flask equipped with a condenser and a magnetic stirrer. 0.04g of AIBN (0.244mmol) was added into the flask and the mixture was slowly heated to 70°C under a nitrogen atmosphere. After radical polymerization for 24h, the resulting yellow viscous solution was cooled to room temperature and precipitated into 300mL of acetone followed by filtration to yield a crude solid. The resultant solid was Soxhlet extracted with acetone for 12h and vacuum dried at 60°C for another 24h to obtain a faint yellow product. The chemical structure of the as-synthesized homopolymer was characterized using 1H NMR.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Fabrication and alkalization of interpenetrating network AEMs
ce:section.ce:para: The procedure for preparation of the crosslinked membranes is schematically depicted in Scheme 1. PVA was dissolved in DMSO and heated at 60°C with magnetic stirring to obtain 20mL of a 4wt% transparent solution. An amount of the crosslinking agent (50wt% GA aqueous solution) was then introduced into the solution. Meanwhile, PVIm and PVBC were completely dissolved in DMSO under stirring to make two individual 4wt% solutions and filtered through 0.45µm PTFE filters. Subsequently, a specified amount of PVIm and PVBC solutions was carefully introduced into the PVA solution. The resulting mixture was vigorously stirred to obtain a homogeneous transparent solution. This solution was then cast onto a clean glass plate, and dried in a vacuum oven at 60°C for 24h and at 80°C for another 3h to form membranes. The resulting membranes were then immersed in a 1M aqueous KOH solution for 48h to exchange the Cl− for OH−. Finally, the alkalized AEMs were stored in deionized (DI) water at room temperature for further use. The as-prepared membranes are termed PP-x, where PP denotes the PVBC-c-PVIm, and x is the mass ratio of both PVIm and PVBC to PVA. A series of membranes (PP-30, PP-40, PP-50 and PP-60) was prepared to investigate the effect of PVBC-c-PVIm content on the membrane properties.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Structure and morphological characterization of the membranes
ce:section.ce:para: The membranes were dried under vacuum at 60°C for 48h before testing. 1H NMR spectra were recorded by Avancell 500MHz (Bruker, Switzerland) using DMSO-d6 as the solvent and tetramethylsilane as the internal reference. FT-IR spectra of the membranes were recorded in the range 4000–500cm−1 using a Nicolet Avatar 380 spectrophotometer (Thermo Electron Corporation, USA). The morphology and microstructure of the membranes were characterized using a field emission scanning electron microscope (SEM, Zeiss Sigma, Germany). The elemental analysis of the membranes was carried out on the SEM equipped with an EDX detector (Oxford Inca). All of the samples were fractured in liquid nitrogen and then sputter gold coated before observation. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was recorded on a PHI QUANTUM 2000 XPS system with Al Kα source. All the binding energies were referenced to the C 1S peak at 284.6eV of the surface adventitious carbon.

The resistance of the membranes was measured by the two-electrode AC impedance spectroscopy method on a Parstat 263 electrochemical workstation (Princeton Advanced Technology, USA). The measurement was carried out at a constant voltage of 10.0mV in the frequency range from 100mHz to 100kHz at a given temperature. Before testing, the OH− form membranes were hydrated in DI water for at least 48h. The testing device with a 1cm×2cm membrane was clamped between two copper electrodes and then placed in a N2-protected chamber using ultrapure water to maintain a relative humidity (RH) of 100% during the measurements. The mechanical properties of the AEMs were measured using a universal testing machine (WDW-1E Testing System) with a tensile speed of 5mmmin−1 at room temperature. A 10mm width membrane sample was initially kept in DI water at room temperature overnight, and wiped with tissue before measurements.

A thermogravimetric analyzer (TGA, SDQT600, TA, USA) was used to evaluate the thermal stability of the membranes. The samples were heated from 30 to 800°C with a heating rate of 10°Cmin−1 under a nitrogen atmosphere. The samples were vacuum dried at 80°C for 24h before testing.

The alkaline stability of the OH− form membrane was investigated by tracking the difference of conductivity after the sample was immersed in a KOH solution. The AEM samples were immersed into a 4M KOH solution at 60°C from 24 to 1320h. After the treatment, the membranes were then placed into DI water for 24h at room temperature before testing. The conductivity and IEC were then measured as described above.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Membrane electrode assembly (MEA) and single cell performance
ce:section.ce:para: The anode and cathode catalyst ink were prepared by mixing Pt/C (40wt% Pt, Johnson Matthey) with 5wt% homemade ionomer in DMF and glycerol. The weight ratio of catalyst to ionomer was 7:3. The resulting mixture was ultrasonically dispersed for 1h and then magnetic stirred for 24h to make a homogenous dispersion. Then the catalyst ink was brushed onto the carbon paper (2cm×2cm) to deposit a catalyst layer with Pt loading of 1mgcm−2 for both the anode and the cathode. The AEM was sandwiched with the electrodes and then hot-pressed at 50°C and 0.8MPa for 5min. Thereafter the MEA was assembled into a single fuel cell with H2 on the anode and O2 on the cathode at a flow rate of 50 and 100mLmin−1, respectively. Single cell performance was evaluated at 60°C and 100% RH using an electronic load (ZY8714, ZHONGYING Electronic Co., Ltd.).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Preparation and structure of the PP-x membranes

ce:section.ce:para: Poly(1-vinylimidazole) was synthesized via radical polymerization of 1-vinylimidazole using AIBN as the initiator. The structure of the as-synthesized PVIm was identified by 1H NMR in DMSO-d6. As shown in Fig. 1, the signals at 1.6–2.2ppm (H1) and 2.8–3.2ppm (H2) are ascribed to the backbone protons (CH2 and CH-). This suggests the successful polymerization of the vinyl group of 1-vinylimidazolium [28]. Likewise, the peaks at around 6.4–7.2ppm are associated with the protons (H3, H4 and H5) on the imidazole ring. The well-defined peaks indicate that the polymerization proceeds smoothly.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Preparation and characterization of the crosslinked PP-x membranes
ce:section.ce:para: After being treated with glutaraldehyde, the PVA solution was mixed with PVBC and PVIm solutions. It is imperative that the mole ratio of PVBC to PVIm is strictly controlled at 1:1 in the mixture so that the benzyl chloride can completely react with imidazole. After vigorous stirring, the homogeneous solution was poured onto glass plates and dried under vacuum to form crosslinked membranes. The EDX spectra in Fig. 2a reveal that chloride element almost disappeared (~0.76wt%) in the membrane, further confirming sufficient conversion of –CH2Cl groups and successful alkalization. A homogeneous dispersion of the two components is important for blend membranes. The compositional mapping images of the PP-50 membrane (Fig. 2b and c) reveal a uniform distribution of the N element in PVIm and the O element in PVA in the membrane [29]. This indicates that the polymers are evenly dispersed in the membrane.

To identify the reaction of benzyl chloride and imidazole groups in the preparation of membranes, XPS was used to record the change of N1s spectra in the polymers. As for PVIm ( Fig. 3a), the N1s peak can be deconvolved into two component peaks, one at 399.9eV and the other at 398.1eV. The former is attributed to the nitrogen through which the imidazole ring is attached to the main chain. The latter is associated with the other nitrogen in the imidazole ring [30]. For PVBC-c-PVIm, only one single peak locating at 400.9eV (Fig. 3b) can be assigned to the generation of the imidazolium cation. The internal conjugation structure of imidazolium cation makes the N1s spectra emerge into a single peak. It is understandable that there is an up-shift in the binding energy after the imidazole was transformed into cations. The results indicate that the crosslinking reaction between PVBC and PVIm occurred during the membrane preparation.

ce:section.ce:section-title: FT-IR spectra analysis of the crosslinked membranes
ce:section.ce:para: Fig. 4 shows the infrared spectra of the AEMs with various PVBC-c-PVIm contents. The spectra display the wavenumber region between 4000 and 500cm−1. Clearly, a large broad band between 3400 and 3500cm−1 is mainly ascribed to the stretching vibration of the -OH groups from PVA or the possibly bound water. The peaks at 2930 and 2850cm−1 arise from the stretching of –CH2 and –CH groups [19]. A strong absorption band near 1148 and 1090cm−1 corresponds to the vibration of C–O–C, resulting from the reaction between the hydroxyl groups of PVA and the aldehyde group in glutaraldehyde [19,31]. This confirms the occurrence of crosslinking reaction in PVA matrix. Additionally, the peaks at around 1540 and 750cm−1 observed in the FT-IR spectrum of PP-x are assigned to the vibration of imidazolium cations [32,33], and become more distinct with increasing imidazolium content. The peak at 1635cm−1 can be attributed to the C=C of aromatic hydrocarbon [34]. All these differences definitely confirmed the successful introduction of PVBC-c-PVIm into the PVA matrix.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Morphology of the PP-x crosslinked membranes
ce:section.ce:para: Fig. 5 shows the SEM image of the membrane surface and cross-section. Typically the PP-50 membrane has somewhat spiniform network on the surface [35]. In the membrane casting process, the crosslinking reaction and film formation proceeded simultaneously. The self-assembly of the imidazolium groups on crosslinked PVIm-c-PVBC chains would result in the formation of the spiniform network phase (Fig. 5a). The cross-section of the membrane in Fig. 5b reveals the formation of a compact and faultless structure with around 20µm in thickness. Furthermore, the PP-50 membrane is transparent and uniform without visible pores (Fig. 5c). Moreover, as shown in Fig. 5d, the membrane could be curved with ease indicating that it is flexible enough for fuel cells.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Properties of the PP-x crosslinked membranes
Analysis of IEC, water uptake (WU) and swelling ratio (SR)
ce:section.ce:para: The IEC, water uptake, swelling ratio and hydroxide conductivity for each series of the crosslinked AEMs are summarized in Table 1. IEC is one of the basic characteristic and reflects the fixed ion concentration or density of exchangeable groups in membranes. The theoretical IEC was calculated from the composition of the membranes with the assumption that the PVBC and PVIm reacted completely. The experimental values were obtained by the back titration method. As expected, it can be seen from Table 1 that with increasing PVBC-c-PVIm content from 30% to 60%, the calculated IEC ranges from 1.31 to 2.63meqg−1, and the experimental values gradually increase from 1.01 to 1.98meqg−1 due to the increment of imidazolium cation groups in the membrane. The titrated IEC lower than the theoretical IEC could be attributed to the existence of trace amount of Cl– in the membranes, as confirmed by the EDX analysis. The designed and titrated IECs in this work suggest that the AEMs possess sufficient exchangeable groups for ionic conductivity.

The water uptake and swelling ratio are equally important parameters for AEMs. Moderate water uptake is necessary for ion migration; however, excessive WU normally generates over-swelling, and is detrimental to dimensional and mechanical stability of the membranes. WU and SR measured at both 30 and 60°C are listed in Table 1. The water uptake decreases sharply from 98.0% to 29.5% at 30°C and from 121.3% to 36.6% at 60°C as the weight ratio of PVBC-c-PVIm increases from 30% to 60%. It is generally known that the water uptake in AEMs strongly depends on the number of hydrophilic cationic groups. More cationic groups mean higher water uptake in polymers. Contrastingly, the results in this work display an opposite trend. As shown in Fig. 6, increasing PVBC-c-PVIm content induces a significant depression in the water uptake at both 30 and 60°C. This interesting phenomenon is attributed to two main reasons. On one hand, higher PVBC-c-PVIm content is accompanied with a denser network, which restricts chain mobility resulting in dense and rigid membranes. Hence the availability of less free space eventually allows fewer water molecules to get wrapped in the pores of the membrane [36]. On the other hand, the amount of water uptake in the blend membranes is directly dependent upon the number of imidazolium groups as well as related to the hydrophilicity of additives.

PVA is known to be a super-hydrophilic and flexible polymer [36–38], and can be easily dissolved in water. Therefore the decrease in PVA content would lead to a low water uptake. A combination of higher crosslinking density and less PVA content rendering the lower water uptake in these membranes is consistent with the trend in recent reports [39]. Besides, the static water contact angle is an indicative of the hydrophilicity of the membranes. The water contact angles stretch from 56.4° on PP-30 to 83.2° on PP-60, suggesting that a higher PVBC-c-PVIm content likely leads to a more hydrophobic interpenetrating network, which is consistent with the water uptake.

The corresponding swelling ratio at 30 and 60°C is shown in Fig. 7. The conspicuous decrease in the swelling ratio from PP-30 to PP-60 is referable to the above mentioned reason. Specifically, the incorporation of the PVBC-c-PVIm is sought to improve the membrane crosslinking density and rigidity, resulting in a lower water uptake, and hence a higher dimensional stability. Acceptable SRs of the PP-50 and PP-60 membranes are observed, and similar to those of Nafion® 117. Therefore, the membranes provide a potential prospect in fuel cell application.

Fig. 8 shows the hydroxide conductivity of the as-prepared membranes. The temperature expectedly has a positive effect on conductivity, probably due to the increase of free volume in favor of ion transport and the mobility at higher temperature. Normally, the ionic conductivity is proportional to the IEC. For example the conductivity increases from 22.9 to 41.1mScm−1 at 60°C with increasing IEC from 1.01 to 1.86meqg−1. PP-60 shows a lower conductivity than PP-50. This is probably attributed to the addition of PVBC-c-PVIm, which acts as both the donor of cationic groups and crosslinking agent. Excessive strengthening of the crosslinked nodes between the PVBC and PVIm chains in PP-60 could have intensified the tortuosity of membranes and impose restriction on the mobility of polymer main chain, leading to a reduction in conductivity [25,39]. What is more, the PP-60 membranes possess the lowest water uptake. This suggests that fewer water molecules were utilized for hydroxide transport. As shown in Fig. 9, the ionic conductivity of the PP–x membranes follows an approximate Arrhenius behavior. The apparent activation energy (Ea) is calculated by Ea=−b×R, where b is the slope of the line regression of ln σ vs. 1000/T plots, and R is the gas constant (8.314Jmol−1 K−1). The Ea of the AEMs varies from 25.18 to 21.57kJmol−1, and is comparable with other reported AEMs [22].

Even without pronounced microphase separation in SAXS (not shown here), the crosslinked membranes exhibited a much lower water uptake and a higher conductivity than other traditional PVA-based AEMs [18,19]. For example, the PP-50 membrane with roughly 39.4% water uptake has a hydroxide conductivity of 21.9mScm−1 at 30°C, and is much higher than 20% (w/w) PVA–PDDA (11.0mScm−1) [19] with 76% water uptake (IEC=0.58meqg−1). Unlike the linear chain polymers equipped with cations in the literature [18,19,37], the existence of crosslinking network containing functional groups makes the membrane effortless to obtain high IECs (high conductivity) and low SRs simultaneously. This definitely indicates that the incorporation of PVBC-c-PVIm could have exceptional promise for fuel cells.

The comparison of mechanical properties between AEMs with different compositions is shown in Fig. 10. The tensile strength of 20MPa with elongation at break of 480% was observed for the pristine PVA membrane [36]. Here, the tensile strength is observed to increase with increasing PVBC-c-PVIm content and to reach a maximum value of 36.7MPa for PP-50. On the contrary, the elongations at break decrease from 61.8% in PP-30 to 5.4% in PP-60 due to the introduction of rigid crosslinking polymers. In addition, the Young's modulus of the AEMs ranges from 355 to 714MPa ( Table 2), and is higher than the crosslinked PVA [36], suggesting their desirable mechanical properties.

The existence of PVBC-c-PVIm helps to maintain good mechanical properties due to the formation of crosslinked network, but excessive amount of PVBC-c-PVIm in PP-60 leads to a reduction of performance probably due to brittleness. Meanwhile, the elongation at break of PP-40 and PP-50 is found to be 43.5% and 13.1% (Table 2), respectively, and is comparable with some other type of membranes [17,18,36]. The network significantly enhanced the strength of the AEMs, and their elongation at break was also maintained at high levels owing to the flexible PVA matrix.

Excellent thermal stability is a fundamental requirement for AEMs in practical application. The thermal degradation behavior of the membranes was examined via thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) in a nitrogen atmosphere. As shown in Fig. 11, all of the membranes generally exhibit three thermal degradation patterns. The first slight weight loss (<5%) below 200°C can be attributed to the elimination of water in the AEMs. The second degradation stage from 210 to 370°C is ascribed to the decomposition of imidazolium cations and side-chain in PVA [22,34]. In the third region, the onset decomposition temperature is above 380°C, which is attributed to the further degradation of imidazolium bearing crosslinked main-chain and cleavage of the PVA backbone. The onset decomposition temperature (280°C) of the PP-x membranes is nearly 70°C higher than that of the pristine PVA and crosslinked PVA samples. A critical observation reveals that increasing the PVBC-c-PVIm content leads to an increase in the degradation temperature and a decrease in the weight loss. The enhancement of polymer network is probably beneficial to the membrane thermal stability [36]. In summary, an improved thermal stability was achieved by the incorporation of PVBC-c-PVIm into PVA matrix and the prepared membranes practically have higher thermal stability than the other PVA-based membranes [25,31].

Besides the excellent thermal stability and high ionic conductivity, the prepared AEMs also exhibit sufficient chemical stability for long-term application in alkaline fuel cells. In this study, the alkaline stability of PP-50 was investigated by immersing the membranes in a 4M KOH solution at 60°C for 1320h. The variation of conductivity was monitored at certain intervals. As shown in Fig. 12, the conductivity decreased by 23.2% within the first 648h. After testing for 1320h, the membrane still maintained around 74.6% of the original conductivity. The IEC decreased from 1.89 to 1.34meqg−1. The decrease in conductivity is mainly due to the degradation of imidazolium groups under high pH conditions. The primary degradation pathway is considered to follow an imidazolium ring-opening mechanism, triggered by the nucleophilic attack of OH– at the C2 position [29]. Fig. 13 shows the FT-IR spectra of the membranes after exposure to the alkaline environment for 1320h. One cannot see any apparent difference in the imidazolium peaks from the original membrane. Some researchers have proposed that some poly(arylene ether) AEMs exhibit catastrophic degradation in an alkaline solution due to the cleavage of aryl- ether from polymer backbone via a SNAr reaction [40]. In this work, aryl-ether bond is absent from the polymer main chain, and thus avoids the degradation of the polymer backbone in an alkaline solution. Moreover, the imidazolium with internal conjugation of the π-electrons is fixed in the crosslinked network in PVBC-c-PVIm. These factors could be responsible for potentially protecting the membranes from the severe nucleophilic attack by hydroxide ions and guarantee the membranes long-term chemical stability.

The PP-50 membrane was used for the single cell evaluation given its high ionic conductivity and desirable stability. The performance of the fuel cell was examined at 60°C with fully humidified H2/O2 under ambient pressure. Actually, a single cell was assembled using Pt catalyst with a loading of 1mgcm–2 in both the anode and cathode. Fig. 14 shows voltage–current density relationship and the polarization curves. The open circuit voltage (OCV) of the H2/O2 fuel cell is 0.94V. A high OCV indicates that good gas barrier property of the membrane is more favorable electrochemical reaction kinetics in an alkaline environment [27]. When the current density increases, the cell voltage drops gradually. This can be explained by internal resistance (IR) losses. Such IR losses are mainly attributed to the preliminary interfacial architecture between the electrode and the membrane. A peak power density of 37.1mWcm−2 is obtained at a current density of 64mAcm−2, and is comparable with other reported AEMs [41,42]. The single cell performance could be affected by several factors such as the surface activity of the electrode and the compatibility between the ionomer used in the electrodes and the membrane. For a better cell performance, MEA fabrication procedure and ionomer preparation need further optimization.

A series of novel interpenetrated AEMs was fabricated in this work by blending modified PVA with bifunctional macromolecular crosslinking agent. The crosslinked polymers not only form a network structure to improve the stability, but also serve as hydroxide conductor to enhance the conductivity. The crosslinked membranes were formed by the precise control of the amount of PVIm and PVBC. The net effect of the rigid crosslinking network and flexible hydrophilic PVA matrix rendered the as-prepared membranes with higher ionic conductivity and lower swelling ratio synchronously. An excessive crosslinking induced brittleness of the PP-60 membrane leads to poor mechanical properties. The PP-50 membrane was tuned to be an optimal AEM. The resultant membranes display desirable performance with water uptake of 39.4%, hydroxide conductivity of 21.9mScm at 30°C and tensile stress of 36.7MPa. Likewise, high thermal stability by means of the incorporation of crosslinked polymers is equally evident. Meanwhile, the PP-50 membrane has a good chemical stability in a high pH solution at 60°C, indicating that the membranes can enduringly fulfill the basic conductivity requirement for alkaline fuel cells. Thus, based on the above results, the viable crosslinking technique with blend method provides a promising strategy to design AEMs for fuel cell applications.
